why.say: Let me start with a question. Our 07/20/2026 Time-Limited Demand to Keystone lapsed unaccepted on 08/21/2026, and the 48-Hour Mandate got no answer. What's our very next legal step, and who decides it? Right: we file suit, and Atty. Thorne makes that call. On 09/24/2026 John Doe's file became Civil Action No. 26-CV-04417, and that changes everything about how we work. An adjuster's deadline bends. A court's deadline doesn't. That's why we keep a Pleadings Log and a Discovery Calendar, and their whole job is to prove, every single day, that nothing filed, served or owed has slipped. Here's our day: litigation support first, then the Property Damage dispute, then deposition preparation, and we finish with liability disputes and MIA clients.
why.ask: What's the very next legal step on John Doe's file, and who gets to decide it?

theory.say: Now, the big shift. A lawsuit is a highly structured, court-mandated process, and if we miss a deadline or misfile a document, the court can dismiss the case. Your role changes by phase. In pleadings you track service and draft the files. In discovery you gather data and prep the client. In trial prep you coordinate schedules and pull the final medicals. And once suit is filed, paperwork stops being admin tracking; a missing document can jeopardize the trial. You'll meet three written discovery tools: interrogatories, which are written questions under oath; requests for production, which demand documents; and requests for admission, which demand an admit or deny. All of them run on strict deadlines. And every filing by either side creates a docket entry whose clock runs whether or not the email ever reached you.
theory.ask: Which of these have you met before, and where would it show up on John Doe's file?

frame.say: Think of the litigation lifecycle in three phases, and I want you to see where you fit. Phase one is pleadings: the Complaint is filed, the defendant is served, and the Answer comes back. Your job there is tracking service timelines and drafting the initial files. Phase two is discovery: interrogatories, requests for production, depositions. That's where you calendar every response, gather the data and meet with the client, and honestly, it's where most of your time goes. Phase three is trial prep: expert disclosures, motion practice, and then trial or settlement. You coordinate schedules and update the final medicals. Every case moves through these three, and knowing which one you're in tells you what your desk should look like this week.
frame.ask: On John Doe's file, which phase is he in right now, and how can you tell?

rules.say: First rule: litigation isn't a longer negotiation. From the 09/24/2026 filing on, the court sets the pace. The Complaint has five parts, caption, jurisdiction, facts, causes of action and prayer for relief; Atty. Thorne drafts it, and before he signs, you verify the filing date against the SOL and the defendant's exact legal name. Service proves the defendant knew, so log every attempt. Still unserved at day 14, that was 10/08/2026, you escalate for Skip-Trace authority. Smith was served 10/14/2026. Read the Answer as a roadmap, and treat RFAs as the danger zone: one unanswered in time may be deemed admitted. When discovery lands, calendar it that day and book a Discovery Intake Meeting; never mail John Doe all 70 requests. And the line: you track, calendar, compile and draft. Atty. Thorne decides and signs, and you never tell John Doe how to answer.
rules.ask: Which phase will take most of your time, and why?

model.say: Take a look at this master timeline. It runs from 09/24/2026 to 01/13/2027, and each numbered badge is a trigger: the Complaint filed, Smith served on 10/14, the Answer on 11/12, discovery mailed 12/01, the Scheduling Order on 12/10, and our own set e-served 12/14. From every trigger, a line drops to its due date. Watch the 12/01 line, because it's drawn in three steps: plus 30 days, plus 3 mail days, and then Sunday rolls to Monday, landing on 01/04/2027. Over on the right is the warning I want burned in: 15 RFAs, unanswered means deemed admitted. Along the bottom sit the five numbered litigation sub-folders. The point of the whole picture is simple. Every date on our calendar is a calculation that anyone can re-check.
model.ask: If I hid the due dates, could you rebuild each one from its trigger alone?

job.say: Let me tell you how this actually runs. Atty. Thorne authorizes suit, and before signature you verify the filing date against the SOL and confirm Robert Smith's exact legal name from an independent record like the Declaration Page or DMV records, not the Police Report alone. It's filed 09/24/2026, well inside our 02/04/2028 internal hard date, and you log it in the Pleadings Log. The stamped complaint goes into 01_PLEADINGS the same day. Then a service attempt fails. You log it, and when he's still unserved at day 14, 10/08/2026, you escalate to Atty. Thorne with the attempt log, run the Skip-Trace on his approval and send him an update. Finally, discovery and RFAs land. You calendar each response with its arithmetic and alert Atty. Thorne within the hour the RFAs arrive, time-stamped.

dodont.say: Time for a game: 3 Clues, 1 Rule. I'll reveal three clues, one at a time, about something a Case Manager did on this file. As soon as you think you know, call it out: Do or Don't. Then the important part, name the rule behind it. Everything here comes from what we just covered: the arithmetic written into every calendar entry, the baseline questions we ask in every interrogatory set, recording John Doe's own words, the SOL, and how we count from a trigger date. Don't just shout the first answer. If you're unsure after clue one, wait for clue two. The points go to the person who can explain why, not just who's fastest.
dodont.ask: Ready for the first clue? Who wants to call it after just one?

why.say: I'm holding up the Scheduling Order. This one page now outranks every adjuster letter in the file. Why? Because a judge signed it, and every date in it is absolute. It was entered 12/10/2026, and it now runs John Doe's case to a 09/13/2027 trial calendar. So how do we make sure none of those dates sneaks up on us? Two tools. A trial-prep checklist turns the order's dates into tasks that somebody owns. And the KPIs prove, week by week, that each of those tasks is ahead of its deadline rather than behind it. That's the whole lesson in a sentence: the order sets the dates, the checklist assigns them, and the numbers show we're winning the race.
why.ask: Why does a single page signed by a judge outrank every adjuster letter in this file?

theory.say: Trial preparation is where you compile the final puzzle pieces so Atty. Thorne walks into court fully armed. Discovery is the heavy lifting. Both sides have to lay their cards on the table, and it's where you'll spend most of your litigation time. Then there's the deposition, an oral interview under oath recorded by a court reporter. You own the logistics, never the testimony. Remember too that litigation can take one to three years, so we rerun records and bills to show the total cost of the injury, not the snapshot from pre-lit. And to keep all of that honest, we run a weekly KPI audit: measurable checks, like a process server assigned within 48 hours, so a slipping file shows itself before it fails.
theory.ask: Which of these four have you already seen show up on John Doe's file, and where?

frame.say: Here's phase three, trial and mediation preparation, and it comes down to three jobs. First, the final run. Because litigation can stretch one to three years, you rerun records from every provider, and you never just reuse the pre-lit package. Second, subpoena management. You draft trial subpoenas for the witnesses Atty. Thorne names, so they're legally required to appear. You don't pick the witnesses; he does. Third, the trial binder. You take the exhibits from the litigation file and index and tab them, so when Atty. Thorne is at the counsel table, he can put his hand on any document in seconds. Get these three right and the attorney never has to wonder whether something's missing.
frame.ask: Looking at John Doe's file today, which of these three jobs is already in motion?

rules.say: The Scheduling Order controls. Pin it to the front of the file with 30-, 14- and 7-day alerts on every date: our experts 03/15/2027, theirs 04/15/2027, mediation by 03/31/2027, discovery closing 05/28/2027, pretrial 08/12/2027 and trial calendar 09/13/2027. Every extension goes in writing: once Atty. Thorne agrees, you draft the same-day confirmation for his signature, in his name. Watch two traps. One is treating court deadlines like adjuster deadlines. The other is letting the client talk to the other side; if Keystone or a defense investigator reaches John Doe, step in and tell Atty. Thorne that day. For the 02/18/2027 deposition, you handle the reporter, the link, the tech check and the packet by 02/11/2027. Prepare the process, never the testimony. And every KPI gets a formula and a target.
rules.ask: Defense counsel will spend John Doe's deposition on the 14-Day Gap. What's your job before 02/18/2027, and where does it stop?

model.say: This is what being ahead looks like. Across the top is the trial-prep runway, from 01/20/2027 to 09/13/2027, with seven milestones: the deposition on 02/18, our experts 03/15, mediation by 03/31, defense experts 04/15, discovery closing 05/28, pretrial 08/12 and the trial calendar 09/13. Before each one you'll see three little ticks for the 30, 14 and 7-day alerts. Notice the red band dropping from 05/28: nothing that needs an answer gets scheduled past it. Underneath are nine KPIs in three families, and every single one has a target you can measure, like 48 hours, 1 hour, 7 days or 10 days. Here's the principle. A KPI without a target is a wish, and stay on top of RFAs isn't a KPI.

job.say: Picture a week in the life. The Scheduling Order is entered 12/10/2026. You pin it to the front of the file, calendar all six dates with three alerts each, that's 18 alerts, and file the order in 01_PLEADINGS. Next, Atty. Mercer's office calls and an extension gets agreed by phone. You confirm Atty. Thorne actually approved it, draft the written confirmation for his signature, send it that same day in his name and recalendar; no scheduling-order date moves without a court order. Then the deposition is noticed. You book the reporter, the link and the technology check, and send the attorney-approved packet by 02/11/2027, confirming John Doe got it. And every week you run the docket audit: each KPI shows its formula, its target and a dated reading, and every miss gets routed.

dodont.say: Let's play 3 Clues, 1 Rule. Three clues will appear one at a time, each a little snapshot from John Doe's litigation file. Your job is to call it, Do or Don't, and then name the rule from today's lesson that decides it. Think about what we just covered: the three alerts on every order date, the 30-day client call, the 10-day subpoena audit, who chooses trial witnesses, setting John Doe's expectations, and what happens with phone-only extensions, pre-lit records and late prep packets. You can call it early if you're confident, but if you're wrong, the room gets to steal it. Naming the rule is worth more than being first.

case.say: It's 01/05/2027, Track B. Civil Action No. 26-CV-04417 is three months old. The docket calendar was audited and corrected on 12/10/2026, but nobody ever reconciled the CMS Pleadings Log to it, and the reconciliation check now shows five mismatches. The executed Affidavit of Service, filed 10/16/2026, is still sitting in an Allied Process Services email with no row. The Interrogatories and RFPs mailed 12/01/2026 share one row that still says due 12/31/2026, while the calendar shows 01/04/2027. There's no row at all for the 15 RFAs. The Scheduling Order is saved as scan_1210.pdf, and a Certificate of Service dated 01/04/2027 sits in Documents, unlogged. I'm putting the log on screen. You've got 90 seconds to tell me what's wrong before anyone touches it.
case.ask: In ninety seconds, how many problems can you find in this log as it stands?

Add every missing row, recompute each response date from its trigger and its method of service, and write the arithmetic right into the row. File each document in its numbered sub-folder with a proper name, and calendar the Scheduling Order's six dates. Then the graded call: the RFA deadline never had its own row, and it's passed. Prove compliance from that Certificate of Service, record the misses honestly, and report to Atty. Thorne today. Partway through, Jenna Price, Atty. Mercer's paralegal, will call. Log her words verbatim with the time, take no position, tell her only that Atty. Thorne will respond, and route it to him. Hand in the corrected, source-linked log and your report.

Did you correct the Interrogatories and RFPs to 01/04/2027 with the count written out, 12/01 plus 30, plus 3 for mail, Sunday rolled to Monday? The 15 RFAs need their own row with a red deemed-admission flag. Is the Certificate of Service logged and checked, signed verification attached? Smith's responses go on 01/13/2027, and remember, no extra 3 days for e-service on this file. The Scheduling Order should be renamed, filed in 01_PLEADINGS, with all six dates. And did you record the late rows as misses, not back-dated, and report to Atty. Thorne without calling Atty. Mercer? One row per set, every row linked to its source.

Put the checklist beside the Scheduling Order and find the first wrong date.

And the graded call is choosing which two items go to Atty. Thorne first.

Records subpoenas return before 05/28/2027, and 04/28/2027 is flagged as the last day to e-serve a 30-day request, confirmed with Atty. Thorne. All six dates carry three alerts, 18 in all. The deposition notice is docketed by 01/22/2027, the reporter confirmed, calendars aligned and the packet set for 02/11/2027. Your Gap Record lists the documents, the EMS report, the Northgate attendance, the texts to Margaret, the MRI read, the Causation Letter, and nothing scripted for John Doe. Work the 12/01/2026 response date step by step, explain how the count changes for a set e-served by consent, and tell me why you'd confirm the court's rule. If your answer is 12/31/2026 or 01/03/2027, stop and rework the count before you go on. Then name Atty. Mercer's three defenses and the evidence on file you'd pull against each, and tell me where the affidavit, the RFAs and the Scheduling Order get filed and named.
questions.ask: Before you start, what are the three steps in counting from a mailed trigger?

summary.say: Now the self-summary, the principles in your own words. Before anyone writes, think about this one: opposing counsel wants two weeks at 4:45 p.m. and says they'll paper it later. Who can say yes? Only Atty. Thorne, and only in writing, the same day. Then your scenario. It's 01/28/2027. John Doe has been unreachable for six days, his deposition is noticed for 02/18/2027, and defense counsel wants to inspect his Civic. Write out your next five actions in order, and next to each one, who owns it. Be specific about what's yours and what goes to Atty. Thorne.

scale.say: Last step. Rate yourself on each competency from 1 to 5, honestly, then submit it for review. I'll be comparing your self-rating with your score, so if you gave yourself a 5 on deadlines but missed the count in Question 1, we'll talk about that gap. That's not a gotcha; it's how we find what to practice next. One thing to remember: UPL is a gate. A strong score doesn't survive an ethics breach.
scale.ask: Where do you expect the biggest gap between your self-rating and your score?

why.say: Look at this gauge for a second. Which number decides whether John Doe's Civic is totaled? Most of you will say the estimate. It's actually the final bill, $9,255.00, after the supplement. Here's why this matters now. On Track B the Civic isn't a side claim anymore. Its Loss of Use and Diminished Value are pleaded in the suit, and every figure we put forward will be tested in discovery. The repair-against-ACV arithmetic decides which measure of damages applies. And the loss-of-use calendar does double duty: it's also the transportation record that explains the 14-Day Gap. Get the car's numbers right, and you're quietly strengthening the injury case too.
why.ask: Which number decides whether the Civic is totaled: the first estimate or the final bill?

theory.say: Property Damage is a cornerstone of civil litigation. It's the law's way of making an owner financially whole after someone's negligence harms their property. And in suit, it cuts both ways. PD can be strong evidence of injury, or it can become the defense's most formidable tool against it. You need two terms straight. Special damages are quantifiable losses, and every PD figure is special, proved by documents. General damages are subjective, like pain and suffering. Valuation is one of the most heavily litigated PD questions, which is why courts lean on set formulas. The key one is diminution in value: pre-loss market value minus post-loss value, weighed under the lesser-of rule against the repair cost, which caps a Total Loss.
theory.ask: Which of these ideas have you already bumped into on the Civic's side of the file?

frame.say: There are three kinds of damages you can recover, and I want you to be able to sort any figure into one of them. Economic, or special, damages are quantifiable losses proved by documents: the repair, tow and storage, rental, Loss of Use and Diminished Value. That's where everything about the Civic lives. Non-economic, or general, damages are subjective: pain and suffering, emotional distress, loss of consortium. Those are claimed on the injury side, not the property side. And punitive, or exemplary, damages exist to punish egregious, reckless or intentional conduct and deter others, think DUI. On John Doe's file, no punitive claim is pleaded. So when you see a number, ask which bucket it belongs in first.
frame.ask: Where would John Doe's $2,016.00 Loss of Use claim sit among these three?

rules.say: The goal is to make John Doe whole: his position before 02/06/2026, never a windfall. The $2,315.00 teardown supplement of 03/02/2026 is structural, the A-pillar, so it shows hidden damage and impact force. Courts generally award the lesser of repair cost or the drop in value, so run it on the final bill: $6,940.00 plus $2,315.00 is $9,255.00, 52.6% of the $17,600.00 ACV, under Keystone's 75% line of $13,200.00. Repairable. Loss of Use is claimable for each day without the car or a paid substitute, at Keystone's own $42.00 a day. Allocate the 78 days from 02/06 to 04/24/2026 once, claim only the 48 unpaid, $2,016.00. Keystone's 30-day cap is claims practice, and arguing it is Atty. Thorne's job. You compute and report; you never tell John Doe what his car is worth.
rules.ask: Keystone paid for 30 days of rental. Why is John Doe still owed anything for the use of his car?

model.say: This is the same threshold gauge from Day 1, now carrying John Doe's numbers. The bar runs from zero to the ACV of $17,600.00, with the threshold at 75%, $13,200.00. The grey chip is the $6,940.00 estimate at 39.4%, and the orange chip is the final bill, $9,255.00, at 52.6%, the jump being the $2,315.00 A-pillar supplement. Underneath is a ribbon of all 78 days from 02/06 to 04/24/2026. Red for the first 12, navy for the 30 days of rental Keystone paid, $1,260.00, then red again for the last 36. Those two red stretches are the Loss of Use: 48 days at $42.00, $2,016.00. Keystone paid for the middle and nothing on either side.
model.ask: Can you find the two red segments, and say what each one represents?

job.say: On the job, it goes like this. The final repair bill posts with the supplement, so you re-run the total-loss check on $9,255.00 in the Property Damage screen, record 52.6% of $17,600.00, and get Keystone's 75% basis on file in writing. Then the rental ends while the Civic is still in the shop. You log every day without a vehicle, period by period, and land on 12 plus 36, 48 days, with no paid rental day counted. When the 09/24/2026 complaint pleads Loss of Use and Diminished Value, you reconcile the figures across the PD screen, the damages summary and discovery, so $2,016.00 and $3,600.00 match everywhere, and any mismatch goes to Atty. Thorne. And when the deposition is noticed on 01/20/2027, you index the PD severity set for his deposition documents before the 02/04/2027 prep session.

dodont.say: Here comes 3 Clues, 1 Rule for this lesson. I'll show three clues one at a time, each a moment from the Civic's Property Damage file. Call it as soon as you've got it: Do or Don't. Then tell me the rule that settles it. The rules you'll need are all from what we just did: which repair figure the threshold runs on, whose rental rate measures a day's use, how the 78 days are allocated, and why the supplement matters to more than just the car. A hint from me: the double count is sneakier than it looks. Take your time with clue two before you commit.
dodont.ask: Who's willing to commit to Do or Don't before the second clue?

why.say: I've written two numbers on the board, far apart: $792.00 and $3,600.00. Same car, same damage. A Civic with an A-pillar repair in its history is worth less than one never hit, and John Doe didn't cause that loss. Keystone's $792.00 comes from a formula. The $3,600.00 comes from a market appraisal. Let me build the $792.00 in front of you, one step at a time: 10% of the $17,600.00 ACV is $1,760.00, times 0.75 is $1,320.00, times 0.60 is $792.00. Each multiplication is a cut, and you can see exactly where. The gap between those two numbers is pleaded on Track B. Our job is to build the evidence. Atty. Thorne makes the argument.
why.ask: Watching the formula, which of those three cuts bothers you most, and why?

theory.say: The law measures property at fair market value. So what a repaired car still loses is a market loss, and you prove it with market evidence, not with how the owner feels about it. Special value to an owner is an exception, not the rule. Now, a carrier formula is claims practice. It isn't a legal measure, and an appraisal built on real market data is how you test it. That only works if you get the carrier's position and inputs in writing, because only a basis on paper can be answered with stronger evidence. And once we're in suit, there's a tool for non-party records: the Subpoena Duces Tecum. Keep it targeted, though. A blanket request invites a Motion to Quash.
theory.ask: Why does a carrier's formula need to be on paper before we can answer it?

frame.say: So how do we value the claim? Three ideas. First, the lesser-of rule: the owner gets the lesser of the repair cost or the drop in market value, and a car that costs more to fix than it was worth is a Total Loss. Second, Diminished Value: the market value a car still loses after a proper repair. Many courts add it on top of the repair, as long as the total stays under the pre-loss value. Third, special value. Where there's no market at all, say an heirloom, some courts use the actual value to the owner, but sentimental value is still excluded. It's an exception, not the rule. For a 2019 Civic, the first two are what we're working with.
frame.ask: Which of these three measures actually applies to John Doe's Civic right now?

rules.say: Diminished Value is what a car still loses after a proper repair, because buyers pay less for a damage history, and many jurisdictions allow it against the at-fault driver. Many courts add it to the repair, under pre-loss value: $9,255.00 plus $3,600.00 is $12,855.00, under $17,600.00. It's a market loss, not a feeling. Keystone's 17c figure comes from a Georgia class-action settlement, not a legal measure. Critique it: no damage, however severe, gets past $1,760.00 on this car, and the appraisal's 20.5% is more than twice that ceiling. The 0.75 tier sits below the top, severe structural tier, and 0.60 counts the 52,300 miles twice. Test our own appraisal too. PD settles only on a property-damage-only release Atty. Thorne has reviewed. You calculate and critique; you never make, accept or counter a figure.
rules.ask: If this Civic had the worst structural damage a repairable car can have, what's the most the 17c formula could pay?

model.say: Now for the face-off. On the left is Keystone's 17c, laid out as a staircase: $1,760.00, times 0.75, times 0.60, landing on $792.00. Each step carries its flaw in red: the 10% cap, the tier, and mileage counted twice. On the right is the market: $3,600.00, backed by three pieces of evidence, the 05/06/2026 appraisal, the A-pillar supplement and the photos. Between the two cards runs a line at $1,760.00, the formula's ceiling, and you can see the $3,600.00 sitting well above it. Along the bottom, in red, is the warning: PD release only, never all claims. The picture makes one argument. The formula simply can't reach the market.
model.ask: What does that horizontal line at $1,760.00 tell you about Keystone's formula?

job.say: Let's run it on the job. Keystone states its diminished-value figure. You don't argue it on the phone. You ask Atty. Thorne how he wants the 17c worksheet and every input obtained, a discovery request or a written request through counsel, and you draft it for his review, so the base, both multipliers and the ACV end up on file in writing. Then the appraisal arrives on 05/06/2026. You audit its method, its data and the appraiser's credentials, write a dated audit note, and index it as our diminished-value evidence. And if Keystone sends a PD release or a check, you hold it and route the release language to Atty. Thorne, so he's reviewed its scope before John Doe ever sees a signature line.

dodont.say: Let's play 3 Clues, 1 Rule. Three clues will come up one by one, each a snapshot from the diminished-value dispute. When you're ready, call it: Do or Don't, and then name the rule. You'll want what we just covered: getting the formula's inputs in writing, where the critique of that formula gets argued, the difference between documenting a figure and giving John Doe a valuation opinion, how far a release can reach, and what the law will and won't pay for. Listen closely to the wording in each clue. Sometimes one small phrase is the whole answer.
dodont.ask: Which phrase in that first clue makes you lean toward Don't?

case.say: It's December 2026, and the requests mailed 12/01/2026 have arrived. Defendant's First Requests for Production, served on John Doe by U.S. mail, ask for every document supporting the Property Damage claim, with responses due 01/04/2027. Atty. Thorne's message is clear: audit the Civic's numbers before anything is produced, flag what Keystone will argue about the unpaid days, and nothing goes out without his review. Now look at the PD screen, untouched since April. The total-loss check was run on the $6,940.00 estimate, 39.4% of ACV. The loss-of-use line reads 78 days times $42.00, $3,276.00. And Keystone still offers $0 for Loss of Use. Something here isn't right. Your job is to find it.

why.say: Every prep session guide starts with the same line: start by calming their nerves. Good advice. But look at the calendar. John resurfaced on 02/03/2027, fifteen days before he testifies on 02/18/2027, by video, from a room the firm doesn't control. So what has to come before any calming? The audit. Before we sit down with John, we need to know everything in his file the defense might use, so Atty. Thorne meets it first. And here's the division of labor I want you to hold onto all module. Atty. Thorne prepares the substance, what John's testimony covers. You prepare the person and the setting, so John walks in calm, informed and ready.

theory.say: A deposition can shape the whole outcome of a litigated case. Atty. Thorne owns the legal strategy, and you prepare the client operationally and psychologically. That starts with a landmine audit: before any prep meeting, you review the file for what the defense will exploit, so counsel sees it first. Why does that matter so much? Because consistency is credibility. The defense will compare John's testimony with his signed answers and his records, and any mismatch reads as concealment. Then there's the courtroom drama myth. Clients expect TV, and showing them the real, ordinary process calms them without any prediction. And remember, defense counsel writes an evaluation report to the carrier on how John will strike a jury, so how he presents matters.
theory.ask: Who on John's side of the file reads that defense evaluation report, and why should it worry us?

frame.say: Here's the shape of deposition prep. It begins with the pre-deposition audit: prior medical history, signed answers and public social media, with any landmines routed to Atty. Thorne. Then three pillars. Pillar one, de-escalate: no judge, no jury, no shouting, and you calm the client with the process, never a prediction. Pillar two, testimony guidelines: pause, tell the truth, stop once the question's answered, drilled only on neutral questions. Pillar three, dress and demeanor: business casual, nothing flashy, limitations told plainly, never minimized or exaggerated. After that comes the technology check, a computer, camera at eye level, light in front, quiet private room. And the day before, you confirm the date, time and link with the client, Atty. Thorne and the court reporter.
frame.ask: Which of these steps is already done on John's file, and which is still waiting?

Thorne: the 14-Day Gap, the 19-day disruption, the three 2021 low-back chiropractic visits, the seatbelt and the degenerative MRI. Check John's signed answers and public social media too, and route any inconsistency the same day. Never tell him to delete a post. His account matches his records because he's reviewed them with Atty. Thorne, not because he learned a script. Then the pillars: no judge, no jury, calm with the process; pause two seconds, tell the truth, stop talking; business casual and plain about limitations. Test the setup with him on 02/16/2027, confirm everything with all three parties on 02/17/2027, and no one in the room, no notes, no messages, not even to you. You explain process and logistics. Every substantive question goes to Atty. Thorne.

You'll lean on what we just covered: why consistency is credibility, what a calm client does for his answers, why everyone gets the dress-code talk, and the traps of surprise records, reassuring predictions, a bad video setup and over-coaching. One warning: some of these clues sound kind and helpful right up until the third one. Kindness that's really a prediction is still a Don't.

why.say: Defense attorneys love psychological traps. Let me try one on you. So it was just the neck stiffness. Is that all? Hands up if you'd say yes. Now look at the 02/20/2026 urgent-care note: hand numbness. That one yes just fenced off a symptom. Here's the thing. Atty. Mercer doesn't need John to lie. A hurried yes to a narrowed list, a guess or an argument does the same damage. His Answer and the records tell us exactly where he'll dig: the gap, the disruption, the 2021 visits and the seatbelt. What meets every one of those traps? Seven general rules and Atty. Thorne's objections. A script meets none of them.
why.ask: Be honest: how many of you would have answered yes to that question?

theory.say: The defense has a simple goal in a deposition: get the client to contradict himself, lose his temper or exaggerate, because each of those damages credibility. General rules protect against that; a script can't. So let's reset some expectations. Defense counsel may ask very broad questions to discover the facts, and wide questions are normal, not attacks. There's a real difference between an estimate and a guess. An estimate rests on what you perceived; a guess claims what you couldn't know, and only the estimate is honest testimony. Remember, a deposition is information gathering, not a battle. Nothing is won there, so the smallest target protects the case. And when Atty. Thorne objects, that's a formal flag on the record protecting the witness, not a sign of trouble.
theory.ask: Can someone give me an honest estimate about John's crash that wouldn't be a guess?

frame.say: These are the seven Golden Rules for testifying. Rule one, always tell the absolute truth, because a damaged case can be saved and a lied-about one can't. Rules two and three: pause two full seconds, then answer in words. That gives time to think, a clean transcript and a window to object. Rules four and five: never guess, and answer only what was asked, then stop. I don't know is a complete answer, and it keeps the target small. Rules six and seven: hold the silence after you've answered, and don't try to win. The deposition gathers information; the legal battle belongs to Atty. Thorne. These are general rules. We teach every client the same seven, and none of them tells John what to say.
frame.ask: Which of these seven do you think John will find hardest under pressure?

rules.say: Defense questions come in four categories: personal background, crash mechanics, medical history and daily life. Clients underreport medical history most, and here that's the 2021 low-back visits. Rule one is the truth, and the prior-injury question is the Liar's Trap; counsel usually has the records already. Pause two seconds and answer in words, since the reporter can't type a nod. Never guess, answer only what's asked, then hold the silence and don't argue. The Is that all trap can fence off the hand numbness, and the complete record, not memory, is the full list. Compound questions fold two facts into one yes; John can say a question's unclear. On an objection, John stops, then answers unless instructed not to. The EMS report, MRI and EDR are Atty. Thorne's to use. You explain rules; you never coach answers.

why.say: Let me read you Robert Smith's Answer. It says the Escape entered the all-way stop out of turn. It says John was unbelted. And it says he failed to mitigate by missing visits. Now, which of those three isn't about John at all? The first one. Entering out of turn is about Kevin Alvarez's driving, not John's. After suit, the defense went after fault and mitigation: the car he rode in and his seatbelt are comparative fault, and his missed visits are failure to mitigate. Here's the difference. Fault can reduce or even bar recovery. Mitigation only cuts the damages the missed care actually caused. Our counter-package answers each one from this file, with evidence that can come in.
why.ask: Which of Smith's three allegations isn't about John's own conduct at all?

theory.say: Comparative negligence apportions fault between the parties, and the share charged to the injured person can reduce, or even bar, what they recover. There are three regimes, pure, modified and contributory, and they treat the very same fault finding differently. So it's the governing rule, not the percentage alone, that decides whether recovery is reduced or barred. Next, liability status. It's accepted, partial or denied, and recording that status with its source shows Atty. Thorne what's still contested. Keep fault and mitigation separate in your head: comparative fault is about the crash, failure to mitigate is about later care, and it only trims avoidable damages. All of this feeds the counter-package, an index that answers each pleaded allegation with evidence that can come in.
theory.ask: Why doesn't the percentage of fault, on its own, tell us what John recovers?

frame.say: Here's the counter-package laid out, one allegation per row. Entered the stop out of turn: that's about Kevin Alvarez's driving, and Ruth Calloway, the doorbell video and the point of impact answer it, with the EDR corroborating. Unbelted passenger: that's about John's seatbelt, and the EDR shows the belt buckled while the EMS report reads restrained front-seat passenger. Failure to mitigate: the 19 days without visits, 04/02 to 04/21/2026, answered by the A-C-T record, the 04/08 call, the extension refused 04/10 and the evening slots. And causation, the 14-Day Gap and the degenerative MRI, answered by the Gap Record: four reasons, the EMS neck complaint and the Causation Letter. Every allegation, a document.
frame.ask: Which row on John's file do you think the defense will lean on hardest?

rules.say: Comparative negligence apportions fault. Under pure, damages fall by John's share, however large. Under modified, they fall, but recovery is barred at 50% in some states or 51% in others. Under contributory, any fault bars recovery. Confirm the governing rule. Record liability status with its source; Keystone accepted PD liability on 02/17/2026, and the Answer now pleads comparative fault. The out-of-turn allegation targets Kevin Alvarez, and whatever the defense says about him, the stack stays $40,000. Unbelted is answered by the EDR and the EMS report. Failure to mitigate trims only avoidable damages, and the A-C-T record answers it. Evidence counts only if it can come in, so record source, witness and custody, and don't rest on the citation alone. You gather and index; Atty. Thorne decides fault, admissibility and coverage.
rules.ask: If a jury finds John 20% at fault, what does he recover under each regime? And at 50%?

model.say: One finding, four outcomes. On the left is the regime table, with two columns: John at 20% and John at 50%. Your eye goes straight to the red cells, the ones that say Barred, and that's on purpose. Under contributory, he's barred either way. Under a modified 50% rule, he's barred at 50%. That's the cliff. On the right are the three allegations, each pointing to its answer already in the file. Out of turn: RPD-26-018842, Calloway and the video. Unbelted: EDR buckled and EMS restrained. Failed to mitigate: the A-C-T record from 04/08 to 04/23. And along the bottom, a reminder: the stack stays $40,000. Every point of fault costs John money, and each point already has its answer.

why.say: Two people went missing on this file, and I want you to look at them side by side. Robert Smith moved before he could be served. John Doe went silent 27 days before his deposition. What do they share? Neither one has a working contact point. And what's different? One is the opponent, and one is our client, and the authority lines follow from that. The tools overlap: Skip-Trace, the process server, certified proof of notice. But who can authorize what, and what we're allowed to say, changes completely. In both cases, the record we keep is what proves our diligence.
why.ask: Smith and John both went missing. What do they share, and what's different about them?

theory.say: Filing a lawsuit means nothing until service. The defendant has to be legally notified, or the case stalls and can be dismissed. And defendants who know a suit is coming may hide, ignore the door or move, which is why diligent, logged attempts matter: they prove the effort. When an address goes stale, there's the Skip-Trace, a background search of utility, employment and address records to find a current address, run only for a permissible purpose. If someone's still dodging, there's alternative service, a court-permitted substitute like mail or posting, and only the attorney can ask for it. On the client side, certified notice gives us a provable mailing record, and paired with email, it shows John was told how to respond.
theory.ask: Why is a logged failed attempt worth almost as much as a successful one?

frame.say: Here's the evading defendant protocol, step by step. When attempts fail, you log each one's date, time and address and follow up with the server every five days. If the address looks stale, then on Atty. Thorne's authority, a Skip-Trace runs through licensed databases checking utility, employment and active-address records. With the right address and the person still dodging, the server varies the windows, early mornings, evenings and weekends, where the court's rules allow. If that still fails, Atty. Thorne may ask the court to permit alternative service by mail or posting. And when service finally happens, the signed affidavit of service gets filed with the court. Never leave it sitting in an email.
frame.ask: On Smith's service, which of these five steps did we actually need?

Service starts his clock, answer due 11/13/2026, and you check the docket weekly. A Subpoena Duces Tecum needs a narrow Exhibit A, and opposing counsel gets notice first. For John, silent since 01/22/2027, run Day 1's No Contact Protocol. The Step 4 letter goes certified mail and email over Atty. Thorne's signature, by 01/27/2027. Withdrawal goes in only if he directs it. Margaret hears only that the firm needs John to call.

why.say: Put the two nets side by side. On Track A, John Doe netted $20,359.92. On Track B, the 07/06/2027 award brings in the same $40,000.00 gross, and he nets $14,713.75. So what changed? Not the gross. Keystone's stonewall turned a $40,000.00 settlement into a lawsuit, a mediation and an arbitration, and that moved three things: the fee tier, the costs and the lien math. John's going to notice that difference, and he deserves to understand it. That's what the Net Sheet does. It shows him exactly why, line by line, before he signs anything.
why.ask: Same $40,000.00 gross on both tracks. What changed to bring John's net down?

theory.say: The Net Sheet is the ultimate transparency tool. It shows the client where every dollar came from and where every dollar goes. A few ideas sit underneath it. First, the common fund doctrine: the attorney's work and costs created the fund, so lienholders contribute their proportional share of fees and costs. That's the basis for our reductions. Second, the double-dipping trap. Carriers audit the file, so the sheet traces every dollar to its source and never mixes funds. Third, fee transparency. Fees can differ by stream and by stage, so we track each stream's fee separately to keep the ledger accurate and explainable. And finally, the Final Payoff Letter. No lien check goes out without a signed letter accepting it as full and final satisfaction.
theory.ask: Why should Peach State share in the cost of a lawsuit it never filed?

frame.say: Here's how the Master Financial Ledger is built, top to bottom. It starts with the recovery summary: the gross by stream, each with its source, so the BI tendered at mediation and both UM awards from arbitration. Next are attorney fees, the fee on each stream, confirmed from the retainer, and on this file that's the 40% tier once suit was filed. Then case expenses, every advanced cost with its receipt: filing, service, mediation, arbitration, the reporter, records, plus the pre-suit costs. Then the provider ledger: charges, payments, adjustments, balance owed and reduction, with only the liens actually owed, and reductions following the fee actually charged. And last, the net to the client, gross minus fees, costs and reduced liens, shown line by line before John Doe signs.
frame.ask: Which section of this ledger is most likely to trip someone up on a litigated file?

Laura Whitcomb's 07/06/2027 award gives Harbor Point's $20,000.00 and Cardinal State's $10,000.00, and with Keystone's $10,000.00 BI from the 03/18/2027 mediation, the gross is $40,000.00. The fee follows the retainer: suit filed 09/24/2026, so 40%, $16,000.00, confirmed by Atty. Thorne. Litigation costs need receipts too: filing $218.00, service $285.00, mediation $1,200.00, arbitration $900.00, reporter $645.50, records $160.00, plus the pre-suit $486.75, totaling $3,895.25. The fund pays only what's owed. Peach State's reduction follows the fee charged, $744.00, accepted at $1,116.00, and Riverton Spine & Rehab accepts $4,275.00. Net: $14,713.75. Nothing leaves trust until checks clear, Payoff Letters are in and John signs. You explain the arithmetic; whether suing was worth it is Atty. Thorne's conversation.
